chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
title: Harlem as a village of great pianists
summary: Freeman recalls Harlem in the 1930s, with Willie the Lion, James P., Fats Waller and Lucky Roberts, safe streets and Sugar Hill.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: You know, in those days, I don't -- I think I prefer life today because I want to go on and I love life, I have so many things I can do, but I must say that that could well have been the best period of our lives, because we were -- Harlem now had become the place to go -- we are skipping a lot, but I am getting into that because that particular anecdote about Dave takes me into Harlem, where we were to hear the greatest pianists ever in history, Willie The Lion Smith, James P. Johnson, Fats Waller, Lucky Roberts. You name them.

And there was a way of life in Harlem, it was a marvelous village in those days. You could walk around there at 4:00, 5:00 in the morning and nobody would bother you and word was out that the white musicians were there to hear the music and everything was fine, not that they would have bothered us anyway. It wasn't that kind of place. There were some lovely places to live on the Hill. Duke Ellington for many years, had a beautiful apartment on the Sugar Hill.
Yes. And there were so many marvelous places to go, there was good food, and people were marvelous to one another, the different races.
There was a feeling that is just gone.
